Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What does it mean when a Google interviewer says, “There is no feedback on this one” after an interview question?
Answer: After an interview, interviewers are required to give detailed feedback according to several criteria. However, over all the time that the interviewer and candidate interact, there are periods when candidates are not judged, roughly the first 5 minutes and the last 5. It can be difficult to detect when the interview time proper actually starts, versus when the interviewer is still trying to build rapport. Likewise, candidates can feel that they are being evaluated as they ask questions, and feel forced to pick questions as a last opportunity to score points versus as a chance to get a candid answer on something they want to know. So, some interviewers like to signal when the candidate is “off the hook”. If a candidate says or does something completely outrageous during that time, the interviewer will still have to report it, but the bar for outrageous is pretty high, like: personal attacks.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Do big tech companies like Google, Apple, Microsoft, etc. care about what university you go to?
Answer: yes and no. If you’re an experienced hire, then where you got your degree from and whether you have a degree to begin with has close to 0 impact. However, as of 2024 my impression is that it’s very difficult to get an entry-level technical position outside of campus recruiting programs, internships etc., which are targeting some specific universities. This wasn’t true a few years ago (ie pre-pandemic) at a time when a self-taught person could get an interview for an entry-level position. Now that self-taught candidate is pretty much expected to acquire experience elsewhere and reach the point where they can apply to slightly more senior jobs.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How difficult is it for senior software engineers to get an interview at Google?
Answer: Google’s “senior software engineer” / L5 is probably in the upper range of what’s understood by “senior software engineer” in terms of work experience. It is quite an achievement to be promoted to that level, and that’s something that happens usually between 5 to 8 years after being hired. By the way, there are people who elect to never go for that level and stay 15 years at L4. There are a lot of places in tech where you can become “senior software engineer” after 2 or 3 years of experience. It’s really up to any organization to determine where to draw the line between junior and senior and what level of experience represents the pivot. The TL;DR is that in order to be invited to interview as a senior engineer, a candidate must have experience comparable to what a “homegrown” senior engineer at Google would have.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How do you interview for software engineering positions when the candidate has no prior experience in the field?
Answer: How would I interview a candidate who has no industry experience, exactly like a candidate who does. They would get the same coding tests and the same behavioral interviews. A lot of the professional experience of a candidate can be used for these behavioral interviews regardless of their actual role. How would I prepare as a candidate had I no experience as a software engineer, well, how I’ve done it when I interviewed as a software engineer from another career. I prepared for the coding test until I felt I was ready. There’s ample material available, much more than when I made that career change. Candidates won’t get a pass just because they had a different job title before, but they also get a shot at it even though they don’t necessarily come from a software engineering background.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How should an interview with a software developer be concluded if it is clear that the candidate will not be hired?
Answer: Let’s step out of the interview room a little bit. Candidate Alice interviews for BigTech co. The next day, she meets Bob for coffee. How are you, asks Bob. Well, I interviewed for BigTech co yesterday, says Alice. So, how was it? wonders Bob. The interview experience is designed, so that we can influence what Alice will say next. “Oh, they were really super nice, but I don’t think I am going to pass. Too bad, because it looked really cool. “ Or “I don’t care, they’re pompous assholes, I won’t take an offer no matter with how many 0s. “ Candidates talk far and wide about their interviewing experience, so a positive or negative experience can have a profound impact on the employer brand. This should inform how to talk to candidates, regardless of their performance.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is the process for someone with no college education to work as a software engineer at Google or Facebook? How long does this take?
Answer: Education gives a leg up for candidates because Google and Meta are actively recruiting in certain campuses. The easiest way is to get an internship and convert it into an offer. But in the general case, you get hired by passing an interview, which takes 2 steps: being invited to interview, and performing well at the interview. Anyone can succeed in step 2 regardless of education as long as they have the skills, and anyone who has the disposition can learn the skills. When you don’t have a degree, it is step 1 which is harder. When I was working at Facebook, I had 2 teammates that didn’t have a college degree. Prior to Facebook, one was a key contributor to an influential open source library, and the other had already a resume more impressive than most people twice his age, having started a sold a business. In my personal case, I had a degree, just not in computer science. But what I had was a well-read blog. This helped enter the hiring pipeline.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Why do liberals think a baby deserves to be killed just because its mother is 10 years old?
Answer: In 2022, a 10-years old girl who was a victim of child rape had to leave her state of Ohio to receive an abortion. This story received a lot of coverage as it happened in the weeks following the overturning of Roe v. Wade, with some people feeling justified that either: So two irreconcilable opinions. Where are the facts though? 1) Abortions among 10-years-olds are extremely rare. Yes, despite articles like “Ohio 10-year-old's abortion isn't a rare exception[1]”. These abortions are so rare there is no official statistics about them. The latest numbers say that abortions when the mother is younger than 15 represent 0.2% of the total of abortions.[2] This doesn’t mean they never happen. But it’s not like 10 years old were lining at abortion clinics under Roe, and that now, they can start happy families. Further numbers: the birth rate to girls 14 and younger in the US was 0.2 per 1000 girls in 2021. And that’s for the whole age group. Fewer than 10% of all girls start menstruating before 11, so pregnancies at 10 are even more rare than that, and abortions are obviously rarer than pregnancies. 2) abortions is not killing babies. embryos, fetuses, babies, three different things, only one of which is born, and that’s the one which is not concerned with abortions. 80.8%[3] of all abortions happen before an embryo reaches fetal development, and 93.5% performed before 13 weeks. I’m not insisting on this because pro-life folks are pushing for different definitions of what’s a human being than the ones we’ve used in the anglo-saxon legal systems for centuries. 3) nobody can force a woman whatever her age to have an abortion. There are states where parents need to be notified or to give consent for an abortion of a minor to proceed, but the explicit consent of the mother - even if she’s a minor, especially if she’s a minor - is always necessary. So, no one is advocating to force 10 years old to have abortions and no one is advocating for killing babies, liberal or not.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Why does Google show Quora answers when you search a question, as if those hold any validity? So many people dont realize how incorrect most answers are. Am I the only one who thinks they should be excluded?
Answer: As someone who has spent a lot of time using Quora and understanding Google Search, I believe I can give a decent answer to this question. When you think of search engines of the 90s, you have that search box where a user is going to enter text, and then after they submit the search, they are going to get a series of links that contain the text searched. This is not how modern search engines work (Google or otherwise). Today, what people enter in the search box is less a phrase to look for in a vast pile of documents, and more a command. Users expect to get something relevant in response to that command. Technically, what people put in the search box is called a query. The first thing the search engine is going to do, “understanding”, is to extract an intent from the query. An intent is a formal representation of what the user wants. To take the quintessential example of Google if a user types “obama height” they do not want to find all the documents that contain the phrase obama height, but most likely want to know how tall Barack Obama is. Extracting an intent is not enough. There are hundreds of servlets which are treating a query and which are either detecting an intent in a query or assigning metadata to the query, such as: how polite is the tone, as this yields different results. So typically, many intents are extracted. Next the search engine is going to rank these intents. Sometimes one intent is overwhelmingly likely, and it’s very unlikely that the user actually meant something else. Sometimes, it’s not as clear cut. So in our example, maybe the user wanted the height of Michelle Obama. Maybe by some logic they wanted to know Trump’s or Biden’s. And maybe, you know what, they wanted to see webpages that talk about “height” and “obama”. OK, so now Google has several intents ranked. What to do next is fulfillment and execution. Fulfillment means that it’s going to prepare answers corresponding to all the intents. Execution means it’s going to actually get those answers from the servers and render them on screen, and is not super relevant for this question. In the case of “obama height”, in google’s parliance there are a couple of intents which are going to be fulfilled, one is “knowledge base lookup” and one is “web search”. Knowledge base lookup means that the user is looking for a well-known facet (“height”) of an well-known entity (“former US president Barack Obama”) is Google’s representation of the world, its knowledge base. BTW the answer is 6′2″, a fact which is drilled into the mind of anyone who works or has worked in Google Search. When there is a “hit” for knowledge base, or really for any of the intents it understands, then Google is going to answer to the intent with a special card. That’s the happy path because if Google actually guessed the intent of the user, then the special card is going to do a much better job at responding to it than expecting them to click on one of 10 blue links. But web search is almost always fired as well, which is the list of blue links with a blurb. So on to Quora content. Quora is used by Google’s knowledge base as one of many trusted sources of information. This doesn’t mean that Google feels that whatever is in a Quora answer is absolute truth. But there is some curation, there is some validation by other users through upvotes and downvotes, so it’s much better than an arbitrary piece of web content. That is not foolproof. A notorious example is when some folks decided to update the height of cartoon character Caillou on the Fandom wiki (another trusted source, due to its human curation). Caillou, a toddler, still comes up as being 5′11″ if you google “caillou height”. Google is well aware that “it happens” and generally doesn’t care as long as directionally, content from trusted sources is more reliable on average. It also has mechanisms to address poor results. As a user you can report an answer as poor (and as a human you can also try to tweak the source of the knowledge base which I suspect is still going on with Caillou). So the answer of your question is that for the queries for which there are Quora answer, Google doesn’t have more authoritative content and it believes it is more useful to the user than just sending them to a list of links. Google also found that more often than not, when displayed, Quora content is actually helpful.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is the reason for the high number of failures in technical interviews at Google and Facebook? Is it due to lack of preparation from candidates, or is there another reason?
Answer: Google gets about 3 million applications per year. There are very few open positions. That’s all you need to know. During a big part of the 2010s, the reasoning behind tech hiring is that someone who is good enough should get a job. This may still be true in some companies that are in very fast growth. In most of the tech world though, candidates are applying for a specific role in a specific team, so there will be a limited number of candidates who will get an offer. This allows employers to move the bar up. So sure, there is a lot of advice out there for candidates, and a lot of it makes sense. But there is no such thing as “the most common mistake” which if addressed will guarantee a spot. At the end of the day, interviews are complex human interactions with a lot of variables in play, evaluations are subjective to some extent, hiring committee is also composed of humans and there are lots of factors that contribute to a decision.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What might motivate someone to leave a large company like Google or Facebook to work for a smaller company like Microsoft or Twitter?
Answer: to give you a certain order of magnitude of what’s a large or a small company, Microsoft has roughly 220,000 employees Google has roughly 180,000 Meta has around 60,000 X corp has less than 2,000. As someone who’s worked at both Google and (then) Facebook I feel that these companies have a pretty similar culture. Google and Facebook/Meta are unique and have their particularities, but for somebody who would leave Google to go anywhere else, Meta is where they would see the least jarring differences. Microsoft is also pretty similar afaik, and so was Twitter 10 years ago, even though it was much smaller. Microsoft, Google and Facebook had a few thousand employees for quite some time before getting very large, and they were still distinctively large tech companies. A lot of folks went from Google or Facebook to Twitter in the mid 2010s, because Twitter was headquartered in San Francisco and San Franciso based tech employees resent having to commute one hour and a half both ways everyday. A lot of people working at Google and Meta are liberals and the workplace is run with a liberal mindset, for instance there are efforts put behind DEI programs and these companies try to prevent harassment, discrimination etc. However, politically the CEOs stay hands off. Zuckerberg had to do a lot of efforts to court conservatives and convince them that his platform wasn’t discriminating against them. All tech companies give money to conservative PACs that otherwise advance their interests in DC. Twitter/X, though, is different, with Musk having bought it for clearly ideological reasons. So IMO for somebody to go from Google or Meta to X they would have at least to be comfortable with this very different culture.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Is it necessary for data scientists and software engineers to go through coding interviews?
Answer: The ability to solve problems with code, which is at the core of what they do, must be evaluated. What we call a coding test has evolved a lot over the past 20 years (especially the last 10). This used to be mostly done on a white board, with trick questions considered a good thing, They are now done over video most of the time, with candidates working in some kind of online collaborative environment, and trick questions are avoided. Because of the relative novelty of remote interviewing which makes very brazen cheating possible, I think the format of the coding test is going to evolve further, and it is possible it will no longer be reduced to having a candidate implement a snippet of code that does certain things in a limited amount of time. That said, individual contributors for technical roles must always be able to demonstrate they can code and code well. Specifically the simple fact of having x years of experience and having worked at such or such prestigious tech company is not enough to establish that the candidate can be successful at the job they apply for. I had some candidates who had a very impressive resume and who couldn’t pass the warmup phase of a coding question.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Do companies like Google care about your algorithm solving skills if you have zero experience building an app or working as software engineer before going through their interviews?
Answer: It’s very difficult to get an interview with Google. There are different ways (all selective) to enter the pipeline but if a person doesn’t have a way to demonstrate they have the skillset prior to interviewing, usually through their experience, they will simply not have a chance to interview.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is the toughest technical interview process among Google, Microsoft and Facebook? Why? What's your experience like if you've been through it before?
Answer: In big tech all interviewing pipelines are comparatively selective and all the interviews are comparatively difficult. The difficulty of an interview exercise, by the way, is irrelevant - whether you ask a hard question to 100 people and want to keep the 10 best, or you ask an easy question and still want to keep the 10 best, being able to complete the exercise or do well doesn’t matter, it’s whether a candidate can demonstrate they have the skillset and that they are objectively better than the bar at which the company is comfortable hiring - bar which is comparable across big tech company. Where you’re going to have more differences is in the ratio between applications and offers, not necessarily between these 3 which are comparable, but between large public tech company who receive millions of applications a year and have to select very few people to interview, using criteria which are not necessarily objective by the way, and smaller tech companies.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Is code quality important to Google interviewers?
Answer: At Google the coding interview is administered by an engineer, who needs to interact with the candidate during the entire time of the interview, making sure the candidate is always unstuck and can show their best work. Then the interviewing engineer has to write detailed feedback and grade the candidate according to 8 criteria, substantiating their grade with evidence from the interview. Then, a hiring committee is going to interpret that feedback to make a hiring recommendation. With that in mind, would that be fair to candidates to not take code quality into account? Between 2 candidates that solve the same problem and finish at the same time and are equivalent on all the other criteria, should one that writes clean and maintainable code have the same evaluation as one that doesn’t?

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Why did Google create a new framework called Angular instead of simply updating AngularJS?
Answer: Once the abstractions of React were known to the world, the cat was out of the bag. React has made a lot of choices, some of which were controversial and got a lot of pushback, but overall, React code was both much clearer to follow and much more concise than AngularJS code. So Angular took a leaf from React playbook but by so doing, also introduced a number of breaking changes. Even though React introduced itself as a “dissenter” and ran against established conventions by both AngularJS and other frameworks like Ember, Backbone etc. I’ve always seen Angular as a more opinionated framework with a clear best way (which I see as a good thing), while React, Vue, Svelte etc. are more “do whatever works”. With that in mind I feel breaking changes were to be expected in the Angular ecosystem. The goal is not to ensure continuity but to maintain a “well-lit path” to writing robust apps.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Is test coverage percentage (unit tests) important to developers at their company or do they just say they care to appear more experienced?
Answer: Test coverage as in the intention to have tests that cover the codebase as exhaustively as possible is really important. When you’re a company and you have systems in production, there will be outages. Those outages have a cost - when your systems are offline you don’t make money, you need to take people off other work to fix them etc, and longer term - image of low reliability, loss of customers... When you leave large parts of your code base without tests, virtually all your outages are due to bugs that should have been caught by a test that was never written. So by declining to invest in tests, you are going to face future costs and that’s generally not a good tradeoff. Test coverage as a metric though is often overrated, because most tests are not useful. Put it differently, just adding tests is not enough to guarantee some form of safety unless you have test strategies, test plans etc. As an analogy it’s as if you were equating: “how full is my fridge” and “how many meals can I prep”. I can write a lot of tests (“go to the store a lot”) such that my test coverage metric is very high (“my fridge is almost full”) but if a lot of my tests are flaky (“oops, a lot of my food is past expiration date and should be thrown away”) or exercise things which are always true (“a lot of my food is high calorie, low nutrition content like candy”) or is just one type of tests (“and I guess the rest of my food is only meat”) then you can’t actually do anything useful with all that’s in your fridge. Whereas if you write a testing strategy (“meal planning for the week”) and test plans (“shopping lists for the grocery store”) you end up with a nice mix of tests that are going to address all the scenarios that you want to cover (“there’s a balance of produce, proteins, spices etc so i can cook all the meals that I planned”). When you execute on your testing strategy, test coverage usually follows but it’s a means not an end.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How should you answer an interviewer when they ask, "Where do you see yourself in 5 years?"
Answer: Let’s pause on that question for a bit and what would be a “perfect answer”. A candidate is a professional, so they have a career. I think it’s a reasonable expectation that this professional takes some time to think of their career and develop a certain degree of self-awareness. So, it follows that they can be expected to set goals - what do they want to accomplish in the next few months, in the next years or longer, what do they not like about their situation they want to avoid, what do they miss, etc. If a candidate periodically reflects on their career, they should have clear answers to these questions, and from then give an eloquent answer to that question. There’s no such thing as a formula that works every time.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How do you respond to an interview question about how you would handle working with a senior developer who doesn't like to explain things?
Answer: Let’s make this question a little bit more generic. A candidate has to explain how they have worked / would work with someone their senior, who doesn’t do what they’re supposed to. This is a delicate inter-personal situation because the candidate can’t just demand that the other person change their ways. There are a number of ways to approach that. Direct feedback can work. It’s the simplest way and is worth trying first (unless there’s a strong reason to think it will not work). Describe the situation, tell the person how that makes you feel, what are the consequences and propose a solution. In our case: something like: “Hey, last week, you asked me to work on task 123. I asked you questions and you said you would get back to me but you never did. I’ve just been here 3 months and I felt a bit overwhelmed, but I tried. I spent three days reading the codebase in order to form an idea of what to do, and when I wrote my code change, when you reviewed it you pointed out in 5 minutes all I had done wrong. From there I was able to come up with a better change within an hour, but if you had taken these 5 minutes for me at the beginning of the week, I could have accomplished so much more.” This rests on the assumption that most people in an organization have the shared goal of having everything work better. However this doesn’t always work, and more often than not the person experiencing that issue is going to have to use a third party - either peers (the 2nd or 3rd time the senior person hears the feedback may have more impact), a peer to the senior person, or the manager. The person that feels that their senior is not collaborating the way they want can also figure out tactics to not “trigger” the undesirable behavior. That’s managing up. For instance, ask the questions in public in an open chat channel or by mail with people on copy.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is the reason that tech companies are so desperate for software engineers yet they make them take whiteboard coding interviews?
Answer: I don’t think the premise is true. 10–15 years ago, Facebook, Google and Amazon couldn’t get the features they needed out the door soon enough, and they invented the modern tech hiring pipeline - professionals in technical roles are showered with perks and paid “market rates” but at the same time the interview is highly selective. Many many tech companies copied that playbook. In 2023, the consensus is - maybe they overhired and maybe there is no short term return on investment on every single hire. Maybe big tech companies could do just fine with 20%, 30%, 50% less headcount. But even then. Let’s go back in time 5 years. The point was never to make it easy for anyone to get a software engineering job and make 200k+ per year. Specifically, interviews were never optimized such that people who can’t pass a whiteboarding test would have an easier time getting a job.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Is it possible to write unit tests for classes with only private methods and properties?
Answer: Your class is always going to have at least one public method, its constructor. In some languages there are testing frameworks that can bypass the visibility of a method for testing purposes and so would let you individually test methods even though they are private. So on the face of the question, yes, but i don’t think it’s a great idea, you should test a class at its effective boundaries, and if there are “orphan” methods ie they are private but never called from another methods so effectively unreachable, then you probably shouldn’t test it - either make it public or delete it.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: A newly hired senior software developer doesn't write unit tests and he said he has tested the code manually, so he would not waste time to write redundant tests. As the team lead, what should I do?
Answer: This is not something to be solved in a 1:1 setting imo. We’re not talking about a matter of personal preference, but what I refer to as “the contract” which binds all developers in an organization together. These are rules that should be decided at the highest level possible - organization/company, failing that division or team. There are certain choices in development which are a matter of personal preference, like what IDE to use (though - not always). But there are choices which are made as a group so all developers in that group are more effective. When joining a new organization I found that a lot of these rules are implicit - for instance typically people “get” that code must be reviewed, and if somebody offers comment these comments must be addressed, even if another developer approves of the changes. But every now and again there is someone who doesn’t agree with the rules or who finds that the rules doesn’t let them work how they want, and they will violate part of that contract, either an implicit rule or an explicit one which has been clearly communicated to everyone. So when you have a person that thinks: rule X must be enforced, and another person that thinks: I shouldn’t have to abide by rule X, having a confrontation between these 2 people with them either agreeing to stick to rule X or not is usually not desirable. This is highly disruptive for the group. For instance if in a team everybody gets their code reviewed and acts on all comments, and one person bypasses that process to get their changes committed by hook or by crook, this makes the codebase worse and less safe - for everyone. What must be established is, is rule X good for the group? Have we decided as a group to follow rule X? if so, then all developers in the group must follow rule X, and if anyone wants to challenge it, they can write a doc arguing why it should be revisited and support it with data. This can be affirmed through group meetings, or at least through more than 1 interaction with 1 person that would disagree with the dissenter. I haven’t spoken about testing specifically so far. A technical organization that doesn’t have a healthy testing culture is going to have a hard time getting somebody to fall in line and write the expected unit tests, and I tend to think - they would have made their bed. But if people understand the value of QA and testing, and if there are explicit rules in place, then good luck to this developer in arguing that adhoc manual testing is good enough. Beyond changing their mind, which is really the long term goal, as team lead I would make sure that reviewers reject all pull requests / diffs / change lists / code changes by whatever name that do not contained the agreed-upon level of testing.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Why does Google sometimes automatically complete your search query with something else? Is this a coincidence or is there a specific reason for this?
Answer: The why is because Google wants you to use their search service. Each query can be monetized, so Google wants as many queries as possible. As such it’s very important to remove friction. Let’s say I want to know when my local Walgreens closes, I could type “when does the Walgreens at 123 main street, San Francisco close?” and not get an answer unless I typed everything exactly right with no typo, but then many queries will be left unanswered. Instead if I type “w” and “a” I will see “walgreens hours” as a suggested search and get the information that I need, in addition to a map to the closest Walgreens with assorted local business ads. (your mileage may vary on that) The how is that Google doesn’t wait to submit a full query to handle it. They build a database of likely queries based on keystrokes and are able to surface these queries as the user types.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How does it feel to get rejected from Google after passing all of their interviews, including the final one with a hiring manager?
Answer: Early in my tech career I interviewed at a company that I really wanted to work at. I had some experience at Facebook where I was some kind of jack of all trades, my role was somewhat in between designer, engineer and data scientist but I wasn’t really either of these things. When I interviewed for that company, I actually never knew the actual role I was interviewing for. I was also completely unprepared, how could I not be. In retrospect, there was no way this could have worked, and yet I was highly confident and thought I had done great. Of course I didn’t get the job and that hit me really really hard. Since that interview, I have done about a dozen interviews - I got some offers, and also got rejected some times. But now that I understand the tech interview exercise much better, well, I can’t say it ever feels great to be rejected but it never upset me as much as it did then. But being unprepared (and btw, most of my candidates as an interviewer came out as unprepared) meant I was a very poor judge of my performance and that my expectations were way off, which set me up for a huge disappointment.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Can you describe the experience of being a software engineer who does not code every day for their job?
Answer: As a software engineer / individual contributor, your career goes (may go) through 2 pivots: in a first phase, you’re assigned well-delimited tasks. You create most value by implementing a solution in code. In a second phase, you’re given problems. You create most value by designing a solution, which you may or may not implement. In a third phase, you’re given nothing. You create most value by determining which problems to take on and why, and getting the planets to align so these problems will be solved, not necessarily by you. As someone who is in the latter bucket, here’s what I do all day: I do write code most days, but I can also go weeks without writing (or at least committing) code. Writing code, or rather having written high quality code / having shipped some valuable piece of code or solved a hard problem through code is essential to building a reputation which is very useful for what is the crux of my job.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How much time does it takes to learn & master HTML + CSS + Javascript?
Answer: 10 years as a ballpark figure. That’s approximately the number of years of practice is takes to make senior software engineer at Google, that is education + professional experience. Roughly put, senior front-end software engineers at Google are good enough to work on any front-end problem, short of completely reinventing large paradigms of the web. The majority of technical decisions are made by senior software engineers, which in turn have a big impact on the way the web works. (Same goes for Meta or Microsoft, even if their titles are different - the experience to impact relationship is the same). But even they don’t know everything there is to know on HTML, CSS or Javascript. One thing that many people don’t realize is how wide the scope of HTML is. There are well over 1000 propositions in flight, dozens and dozens of existing web APIs that most people never heard of let alone used, and several possible “futures” of the web. CSS and HTML are pretty much conjoined at the hip, so advanced knowledge of one presupposes knowledge of the other. The coding part of web is a different animal because it’s not “just” JavaScript (which is also very much a living language with a rapidly changing syntax) but also type management, frameworks like React/Angular, the web server layer, modules/bundlers, performance tuning, testing, browser internals, back end integration etc.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is a code review? What kind of questions would be asked during a code review for a dev job with Google, Facebook, etc.?
Answer: A code review interview is an interview where the candidate is shown a piece of problematic code and they have to discuss what’s wrong with it. At Google, It is given to engineering managers, on the assumption that it gives similar signal to a coding interview, but is more fair to EMs who haven’t been coding regularly.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Do you have any tips or tricks that helped you get through a Google interview? How did you pass your interviews with them (SWE)?
Answer: Yeah, prepare. I’ve been an interviewer more often than a candidate. Candidates fall into 3 buckets: In an ideal world, all candidates would be in the first bucket, alas most of my google candidates were in the 2nd with some in the 1st and some in the 3rd. If you are very underskilled for a role, there’s really nothing you can do. The system is designed to reject you. There’s no crash course that will make you likely to pass, and do not give money to anyone who pretends otherwise. You really need the experience expected for the role. If you feel you’ve adequately prepared, there’s nothing much you can do besides resting well, being present and engaged during the interview and hope that you “see” the problem quickly. If that helps, be assured that your interviewers would much rather pass you than fail you. But if you are in the larger group that has a lot of relevant experience and feel you can just wing it, consider spending a serious amount of time preparing. It’s just one of those situations. If you’re going to do a presentation in front of 500 people you do slides and rehearse. Yeah you may know what you’re talking about, but will it be better if you rehearse or not? If you’re going to run for a marathon, you run every week to build the capacity. Yeah you have run one 10 years ago, and you’re still in shape, but aren’t you maximizing your chances of finishing (and minimizing risks of injury) if you prep? If you have an exam coming up, you read the textbook, even though you paid attention in class. Etc, etc. Do yourself a service and prepare.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is the reason that recruiters never give feedback on why candidates are rejected, even when requested? How can candidates best respond to this behavior?
Answer: 1) the main reason is legal exposure. Many (most?) candidates belong to one or several protected categories. If a rejected candidate uses the feedback to sue for discrimination, even if they lose, this will cost money for the company, 2) this is no longer the norm afaik. In my last cycle as a candidate, I was regularly offered feedback when not extended an offer. 2 things are being balanced by HR department - the expected cost of a lawsuit, given that such lawsuits are pretty unlikely, and the expected “employer brand” benefits of giving candidates a good experience whether they pass or fail the interview. 3) Yet, I would still argue that feedback after not getting an offer is a complete waste of time and resources. If I work at company A, and I ask for feedback from coworkers a, b and c, and coworker b gives me constructive feedback - what I can improve - I want to take it to heart, because b and I we really share the same goals - the best possible outcome for company A, and I can reasonably assume good intentions from b towards me. So, feedback from b may lead me to work better. Now, if I work on something which is public facing for A, and there’s a person x who says they hate A and they will never buy their products and the product I work on at A is stupid and everybody that works there should quit, then I can safely completely ignore that feedback. I don’t work for x, we have 0 shared interests, they don’t have good intentions towards me. (And as someone who worked at Facebook and Uber, this is not a hypothetical situation). When a recruiter for a company that didn’t hire me shares feedback with me, we are more in the 2nd scenario than the first. They are going to be nice to me but they don’t have a vested interest in my success, more than any other candidate. The feedback I am going to get is not going to help me succeed better at other interviews, because all companies use different criteria and the interviewers are different and the exercises are different.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Do people who have worked at Google and Facebook regret leaving their former employer (or vice versa)?
Answer: I worked at both Facebook and Google. If you ask me, rationally, whether I miss working at Facebook or Google my answer is a definite no. I don’t miss the perks, which I once enjoyed. I don’t miss early access to the products. I don’t miss feeling in “team Facebook” or “team Google” when either of these companies were having a bad PR moment. I definitely do not miss the work. I have no shares of either companies. At a micro level I do miss the people, as the people who end up in these companies have had a very interesting journey and I also miss the camaraderie. But over the past 10 years, I sometimes dreamt of being back on the facebook bus (which was not the most fun part) or back on either campus. I guess there’s always going to be a tiny part of me that’s going to always be jckr@google.com or jckr@facebook.com. At the same time, I’m well aware that the organizations i worked for are gone forever. I joined Facebook when it had just a couple of thousand employees, and Google when it was still pre-pandemic with people coming 5 days a week to a busting campus. Unless someone invents a time machine, there’s no way to ever experience that again.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is the correct order of software testing: unit testing or integration testing?
Answer: Integration tests, or other large scale tests, exercise a large portion of the code in one go. So in order to gain “testing coverage” quickly, just one test can cover 30, 50% or more of a system. The main problem with integration tests though is that it is typically difficult to come up with all the scenarios you should care about and for which you should write tests. I’ve read many incident reports where the conclusion was that an integration test could have caught the bug, sure, but then again the right test would have to be written to begin with and it was not trivial to come up with the idea of exactly what to test. With unit tests though, it’s easier to go through every possibility and make sure that a function, a class, a file etc. is properly tested - not that just every line of code is covered, which should be a by-product of good testing, but that every which way we’re going to use that code is addressed by a test. If a bug could have been caught by a unit test, then it absolutely should have been caught by a unit...

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is your opinion on not having any questions to ask an interviewer after the interview is over?
Answer: it’s the candidate’s privilege, but it’s a lost opportunity. If extended an offer, the candidate is asked to make a life-changing decision, and that’s the best time to get the most unbiased information to support that decision one way or another.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Is being good at games a requirement for working as a video game tester?
Answer: No. When people talk about video game tester they usually mean quality assurance teams. These folks are given a scenario and need to execute it and report things not working as expected. I’ve never met a tester that wasn’t at least decent at videogames because the recruitment is kind of self-selective, people who are willing to play the same half-baked videogame level over and over all day and who are excited to receive a new half-baked videogame level are interested in gaming and they are good at it. But in the game development process the design team may want to do user research and they may want to hear from highly skilled players, like competitive players. i.e. if I’m building a team-based battle royale shooting game, a market which is both very though to crack and very lucrative to lead, then I very much care about the experience of very experienced and highly skilled players of competing, existing games. But “testing” / “QA” refer specifically to addressing bugs.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Is it common for people who work at Google to have been rejected by other top tech companies such as Facebook, Amazon, and Microsoft?
Answer: It’s not something that we discuss much. The “canon” career for software engineers at Google is get an internship in college, start working there right after school, and spend many years there. Most of the people I worked with had followed that pattern. That’s anecdotal evidence though. I can tell you with very high confidence that the vast majority of engineers at Google, if asked to interview for a similar position at Facebook, Amazon and Microsoft, or reinterview for their current role, would fail at least once. That doesn’t mean they’re bad, but the interviews are designed to filter out false positives, and besides the behavioral interviews for these companies value different traits.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: If someone feels stuck in their career as a software Test engineer, how can they make the transition to full development?
Answer: Different people understand different things by testing engineer. At Google there were various technical people who were 100% focused on testing and who had different titles, and which may be called “test engineers” in other organizations. People who did manual QA were contractors, and it would be extraordinarily difficult for them to become full-time employee, software engineers, though if they have the skillset, they would still have a leg up compared to other candidates. It would also be difficult for people who coordinate these tests (who are full-time employees, and who have a role similar to program managers) to transfer to an engineering role, but still possible and at any rate, they could pick up software engineering tasks and become an engineer in anything but by name. On the other hand, the Googlers whose title was test engineer are peers to software engineers. An analogy would be dentists to other medical doctors. It’s just another specialty. Test engineers focus on coming up with testing strategies and solving some technical problems around testing. There is a regular flow of people who transfer from test engineer to software engineers, and in the other direction.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Can a single person develop a video game by himself?
Answer: Yes, there are many examples. Whether they can develop a successful game is another question. There are 2 obstacles to a solo developer. 1) the sheer amount of work that a game represents and the variety of roles that are involved now. In 2024, a AAA game may have a development budget around $100m. If you assume a (generous) cost of $200k/developer/year, that’s 500 people-year of development. In other words, it would take a single person 500 years. And you need writers, artists, musicians, programmers, level designers, testers, etc. so the solo developer needs to wear all of these hats. Even with much less ambitious projects a game is still a huge amount of work. 2) there’s a ton of competition around games and even in the independent category. Your typical gamer is maybe aware of 5, maybe 10 games which will come out in the next year. But there are thousands and thousands of projects being released each year and it’s very difficult to emerge from the crowd.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Can an HR ask why you left your last job during the interview process? If yes, what is a proper response to this question?
Answer: Yes. An interviewer can ask you that. This is not a question that is going to lead to discrimination. Whether they should ask this question is a different matter, as the answer is probably not going to be useful for their decision to hire or not. The mental model of interviewers who think this question is useful (of which there are many) is that this helps raise a “red flag” which otherwise would have gone undetected, for instance, a candidate can volunteer that they have done something really reprehensible in their last job and you would dodge a bullet by not hiring the...

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Does Google reject candidates who perform poorly in interviews, even if they have a high score on technical questions?
Answer: A pattern that I’ve observed at Google and elsewhere is that a candidate that does great in technical rounds but not in behavioral interviews will typically be rejected. This is not a 100% rule, this obviously depend on the exact feedback of behavioral interviews and technical rounds, versus just a score. But candidates should appreciate that technical rounds, especially coding rounds, only capture a fraction of the skillset a tech company value in an engineer, even though they tend to be more precise or not overly rely on the skill of the interviewer. Conversely, the behavioral round is usually where candidates can show how they communicate, how they work with others, how they understand organizations, their degree of self-awareness, whether they have internalized bad behaviors etc. which have an outsized importance in the hiring decision. It’s unusal for more junior engineers to do really bad at a behavioral interview but conversely it’s challenging for a senior+ engineer to do well. A very common scenario is that a candidate that has enough years of experience to be a senior engineer isn’t promoted to that level at their company because they don’t have the skills, so they interview to get a role at the level they think they deserve, and the interview is precisely designed to spot a light at these cases and weed out the folks who cannot demonstrate they have acquired these skills. That said again this is not 100% rule, every individual case is different and is discussed as is. Going back to the specific case of Google, they collect more information on each interview than any other company I worked at, and everything is weighted in the final decision.
